name: Cherry Tomato
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep for seeds, or plant transplants deep enough to cover the first set of true leaves.
description: A small, sweet tomato variety that grows in clusters. Typically indeterminate and requires support.
tips: Provide sturdy support as they can grow quite large and produce heavily. Water consistently to prevent cracking. Pruning suckers can improve air circulation.
pruning: Most cherry tomatoes are indeterminate. Remove 'suckers' (small shoots that form in the 'V' between the main stem and a branch) to improve air circulation, though some gardeners leave them for a higher yield of smaller fruits.
succession: One planting is usually sufficient for a season-long harvest due to their indeterminate nature.
yield: High yield, can produce hundreds of tomatoes per plant.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when clusters of tomatoes are fully colored and firm. They often ripen in quick succession. Pick frequently to encourage more production.
containerGardening: Excellent for containers. Use at least a 5-gallon pot with a tall cage or stake. Requires consistent watering.

soil.type: Well-drained, loamy soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Benefits from added calcium to prevent blossom-end rot.

temperature.notes: A warm-season crop. Fruit will not set at temperatures consistently below 55°F or above 90°F.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store at room temperature, not in the refrigerator. Can be frozen whole, dehydrated, or canned for long-term preservation.

name: Beefsteak Tomato
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep for seeds, or plant transplants deep enough to cover the first set of true leaves.
description: A large, meaty tomato variety, perfect for slicing. Most are indeterminate.
tips: Provide very strong support due to the heavy fruit. Mulch heavily to retain moisture and prevent soil splash. Thinning fruit can lead to larger individual tomatoes.
pruning: Pruning suckers is highly recommended to direct the plant's energy into developing large fruits and to improve air circulation, which helps prevent disease.
succession: Not typically needed due to long harvest period of indeterminate plants.
yield: Lower yield in number of fruits than other varieties, but much larger fruit.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when fruit is fully colored and firm with some give. Due to their size, it may be best to use two hands to support the fruit while twisting or use pruners.
containerGardening: Challenging due to size, but possible with a very large (15-20 gallon) container and extremely sturdy staking. Consistent watering and feeding are critical.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil high in organic matter.

temperature.notes: A warm-season crop. Fruit will not set at temperatures consistently below 55°F or above 90°F.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store on the counter at room temperature. Because of their size, use quickly after slicing. Can be frozen (sliced or whole) or canned.

name: Cucamelon
description: A small, grape-sized fruit that looks like a tiny watermelon and tastes like a cucumber with a hint of lime. In warm climates (zones 7+), the plant can be a perennial, growing back from its underground tuber.
tips: Grow on a trellis at least 4-6 feet tall to save space and make harvesting easier. The plant is drought-tolerant once established but produces best with consistent water. In cooler climates, you can dig up the tuber and store it over winter like a dahlia.
succession: For a long and heavy harvest, plant a new batch of seeds every 3-4 weeks through late spring.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when fruits are firm and about the size of a grape. They should detach easily. Harvest regularly to encourage more production.
containerGardening: Ideal for containers. Use at least a 5-gallon pot with a trellis of at least 4-6 feet. The plant will produce underground tubers, so give it room.

temperature.notes: Loves warm weather. Very frost sensitive.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage: Store in the refrigerator for up to a week. They are excellent for pickling or adding to salsas.

name: Blueberry
plantingDepth: Plant at the same depth it was in the nursery pot. Do not plant too deep or bury the crown.
winterChill: Most highbush varieties require 800-1000 chill hours below 45°F. Low-chill varieties like Southern Highbush are available for warmer climates.
pruningSchedule: Prune in late winter/early spring while dormant. For the first 2-3 years, remove only dead, damaged, or crossing branches. On mature plants, also remove 1-2 of the oldest, least productive canes each year to encourage new growth.
description: A perennial shrub producing sweet, antioxidant-rich berries. Requires acidic soil to thrive.
tips: Plant at least two different varieties for better pollination and a larger harvest. Mulch heavily with acidic materials like pine needles or oak leaves to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Use netting to protect ripening berries from birds.
succession: Not applicable. Plant early, mid, and late-season varieties to extend the harvest period over several months.
harvestInstructions: Berries ripen over several weeks. Harvest only fully blue berries with a light, powdery bloom. They should come off the stem with a gentle tug. Taste a few to check for sweetness before a large harvest.
containerGardening: Compact or half-high varieties are suitable for large containers (15-20 gallons). Use an acidic potting mix for azaleas and rhododendrons. Regular watering is critical as they have shallow roots.

soil.type: Acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Requires acidic soil. Amend with elemental sulfur or use acidifying fertilizers if soil pH is too high.

temperature.notes: Cold-hardy perennial. Most varieties require a specific number of winter chill hours to produce fruit.

environmentalAlerts.message: Provide extra water and shade during extreme heat.

storage: Store unwashed berries in the refrigerator for 7-10 days. For long-term preservation, they freeze exceptionally well and are perfect for jams, syrups, and baking.

name: Raspberry
plantingDepth: Plant shallowly, with the crown about 1-2 inches above the soil line.
winterChill: Requires 800-1600 chill hours, depending on the variety.
pruningSchedule: For summer-bearing: after harvest, prune the canes that just fruited (floricanes) to the ground. For everbearing: in late winter, prune the top portion of canes that fruited last fall; these will produce a summer crop, after which they should be removed.
description: A perennial cane fruit producing sweet-tart berries. Available in summer-bearing and everbearing varieties.
tips: Install a trellis system for support and to improve air circulation. Use netting to protect ripening berries from birds. Canes are biennial: they grow one year (primocanes) and fruit the next (floricanes).
succession: Not applicable. Plant both summer-bearing and everbearing varieties to get a harvest in summer and another in fall.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when berries are deeply colored and pull easily from the central core (receptacle). Pick every couple of days, preferably in the morning.
containerGardening: Possible in large containers (10+ gallons) with a trellis, but requires diligent watering and winter protection for the pot in cold climates.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Good drainage is essential to prevent root rot.

temperature.notes: Hardy perennial. Tolerates cold winters well.

environmentalAlerts.message: Late spring frosts can damage blossoms and reduce yield.

storage: Extremely perishable. Store unwashed in a single layer in the refrigerator for 1-2 days. For long-term, freeze on a baking sheet before transferring to a bag. Excellent for jams.

name: Blackberry
plantingDepth: Plant at the same depth as it was in the nursery pot.
winterChill: Typically requires 200-500 chill hours. Less than most raspberries and blueberries.
pruningSchedule: In late winter, prune side branches (laterals) on the floricanes back to 12-18 inches. In summer, tip-prune new primocanes when they reach 3-4 feet to encourage branching. After fruiting, remove the old floricanes that have died back.
description: A thorny or thornless perennial cane producing large, sweet-tart berries. Very vigorous and productive.
tips: Wear gloves when harvesting thorny varieties. A sturdy trellis is essential to manage the vigorous canes. Use netting to protect ripening berries from birds.
succession: Not applicable. Choose varieties that ripen at different times to extend the harvest season.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when berries are fully black, plump, and lose their high gloss. A ripe berry will be sweet, not tart, and should pull easily from the plant with its core (receptacle) intact.
containerGardening: Thornless, erect varieties can be grown in large (10-15 gallon) pots with a sturdy trellis. Regular pruning is necessary to maintain a manageable size.

soil.type: Well-drained soil with good organic content.
soil.notes: Tolerates various soil types but prefers slightly acidic conditions.

temperature.notes: Hardy perennial but flowers can be damaged by late frosts.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover plants if late frost threatens during flowering.

storage: Store unwashed in the refrigerator for 3-5 days. They freeze well and make excellent jams, syrups, and pies.

name: Grape
plantingDepth: Plant at the same depth or slightly deeper than it was in the nursery pot.
description: A perennial vine producing clusters of sweet fruit. Takes several years to establish and produce significant harvest.
tips: Requires a strong trellis system. Annual pruning is critical for fruit production; grapes fruit on new growth from one-year-old canes.
succession: Not applicable. Plant different varieties (e.g., table, wine, early, late) for different uses and harvest times.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when grapes are fully colored, have a slight bloom, and are sweet to the taste. They do not ripen after being picked. Harvest entire clusters with pruners.
containerGardening: Possible in very large containers (20+ gallons) with a sturdy trellis, but yield will be limited. Requires careful water and nutrient management.
rootstockInfo: Many grape varieties are grafted onto rootstocks that are resistant to pests like phylloxera and tolerant of specific soil conditions (e.g., clay, drought).
trainingSystems: Common systems include Cane Pruning (like Guyot) and Spur Pruning (like Cordon), depending on the grape variety's fruiting habit.
pollinatorRecommendations: Most grapes are self-fertile, but some varieties may benefit from cross-pollination with another variety blooming at the same time.
dormantSeasonCare: The most important task is pruning, which is done in late winter. This controls the size of the vine and determines the number of fruit clusters for the coming season. Also a good time to apply dormant oil spray.

soil.notes: Good drainage is critical. Avoid heavy clay or waterlogged soils.

temperature.notes: Cold hardiness varies by variety. Requires warm summers for fruit ripening.

environmentalAlerts.message: Late spring frosts can damage new growth and flowers.

storage: Store unwashed grape clusters in a perforated plastic bag in the refrigerator for 1-2 weeks. Can be frozen for long-term use or made into juice or jelly.

name: Apple
plantingDepth: Plant with the graft union 2-3 inches above the soil line.
description: A fruit tree producing crisp, sweet apples. Requires cross-pollination from another apple variety for fruit production.
tips: Plant at least two different varieties that bloom at the same time for pollination. Annual pruning is essential for tree health and fruit quality.
succession: Not applicable. Plant different varieties (early, mid, late season) to have apples for an extended period.
harvestInstructions: Harvest when apples are fully colored and easily twist off the branch with an upward lift. Taste for ripeness. Different varieties ripen at different times from late summer through fall.
containerGardening: Only dwarf or super-dwarf rootstocks are suitable for very large containers (25+ gallons). Requires significant pruning and care.
rootstockInfo: Apple trees are grafted onto rootstocks that control the tree's size (dwarf, semi-dwarf, standard), disease resistance, and cold hardiness.
trainingSystems: Common systems include Central Leader for standard trees, and Espalier or Tall Spindle for high-density or ornamental plantings.
pollinatorRecommendations: Requires a different apple or crabapple variety that blooms at the same time for cross-pollination. Some varieties are 'triploid' and cannot pollinate others.
dormantSeasonCare: Prune in late winter to remove dead or crossing branches, improve light penetration, and maintain a strong structure. Apply dormant oil sprays to control overwintering pests.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil with good organic content.
soil.notes: Avoid poorly drained or compacted soils.

temperature.notes: Requires winter chill hours for proper flowering. Very cold hardy.

environmentalAlerts.message: Late frosts during bloom can severely reduce fruit set.

storage: Store in a cool, dark, humid place like a root cellar or refrigerator for 2-6 months. Can be processed into applesauce, cider, or dried slices for long-term preservation.
